title: A Screen Isn't Human. Neither Is a Book.
author: Zach Groshell
summary: Zach Groshell mounts a careful evidence-based challenge to the 'abstinence movement' in education — the growing push to ban not just personal devices but all screens from classrooms. While sympathetic to phone bans and the concern that teachers misuse technology as a digital babysitter, Groshell argues that blanket prohibitions rest on weak evidence and intellectually lazy reasoning. The meta-analytic literature on screen time and academic performance is largely correlational, dominated by self-report surveys, and fails to disaggregate recreational from academic screen use; academic screen use actually correlates positively with achievement. Experimental research on educational technology shows small, uneven positive effects — exactly what we would expect if the quality of instruction, not the medium, drives outcomes. The real problem Groshell identifies is not the technology itself but the pedagogical vacuum it fills: Chromebook-as-babysitter is a symptom of activity-based rather than objective-based lesson planning. He extends the argument with a memorable comparison: a book is also not human, also does not love a child, yet no one proposes banning books. The appropriate question is never 'screen or no screen?' but 'what is on the screen, what are students thinking about, and are they learning?' Groshell closes by noting that scalable instructional systems using well-designed technology could teach far more children powerful knowledge than has ever been possible — an opportunity that over-correction would forfeit.
points: The core empirical case against screens collapses when you disaggregate the data: the large meta-analytic studies find that overall screen media use is not significantly associated with academic performance, and the negative correlations that do appear cluster around recreational use — television and video games — not academic use, which correlates positively with achievement.

The 'teachers use it poorly' objection cuts both ways: teachers use read-alouds, exit tickets, seating charts, and direct instruction poorly as well. Banning technology because it is misused by some teachers would equally justify banning books, feedback, and anything else that poor pedagogy can degrade.

Groshell identifies the Chromebook-as-babysitter problem as a downstream symptom of a deeper pedagogical failure — organizing instruction around activities rather than objectives — making the device an easy scapegoat for what is actually a theory-of-instruction problem.

The abstinence position is, in Groshell's framing, intellectually lazy because it sidesteps the substantive questions: what program of skills are students mastering, what is the theory of instruction within the app, is there error correction and feedback? These questions require knowing something about cognitive science and curriculum design.

The comparison of a book to a screen is the rhetorical turning point of the article: neither is human, neither loves the child, neither replaces the teacher-student relationship, yet we understand that great books extend what great teachers can do — the same logic applies to well-designed educational technology.
quotes: Screen time is associated with negative outcomes. Associations are correlational, and the causal research on this topic is thin. If you go look at what people are citing, the case is built almost entirely on cross-sectional surveys where kids (or their parents) self-report how many hours they stared at a screen, and then somebody runs a correlation against test scores or grades.

When I read the largest one (Adelantado-Renau et al., 2019, pooling 58 studies and over 100,000 kids) the headline finding was that overall screen media use is not significantly associated with academic performance at all (ES = −0.29, 95% CI −0.65 to 0.08, confidence interval crosses zero). The negative associations they did find were specific to television viewing (ES ≈ −0.19) and video game playing (ES ≈ −0.15) — not 'screens' as a category.

As someone who observes lessons for a living, this is what I see daily — there is no purpose for the use of the technology, there is no systematic program of skills that the kids are mastering, there is no sophisticated 'Theory of Instruction' within the apps, and there is no rhyme or reason for this shitty tech. It is just there to make the day go by a little faster for the teacher, and maybe for the students too.

A book does not love the child reading it. A book does not kneel down to a child's eye level. A book does not dry shoes that have been rained on, nor notice when a kid hasn't eaten. A book does not remember that this particular child's dad just deployed.

A book is a static, mass-produced artifact that was manufactured by strangers and shipped to a school where it sits on a shelf until a teacher pulls it down. By every standard the abstinence movement applies to a screen, a book should also be banned.

This is why the abstinence position is intellectually lazy. It skips the real questions: what are we putting in front of students, what are they thinking about, and are they learning? The ban-it-all crowd does not want to have that conversation, because having it requires them to know something about instruction, about mastery, about curriculum, about cognitive science, and to confront the fact that many kids are getting extremely subpar paper-pencil lessons, day after day, week after week.

What about the parent — new to this country, watching their kid struggle — who realizes early on that the only way to get a baseline of facts taught properly, through direct, explicit instruction, is to hire a tutor they cannot afford? Meanwhile, the public school they've been assigned to serves up a smorgasbord of romantic social-emotional mumbo jumbo, telling kids that knowledge isn't important, and that all you need to do is, ironically, 'look it up' in the age of AI.
